analysis.one_liner: Lets an independent safety board enforce health and safety rules at nuclear weapons plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended, after the Energy Department filed an unfavorable review.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have turned the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board from an advisory panel into a real regulator over the Department of Energy's nuclear weapons plants. It could have written binding safety standards, required licenses before new or modified facilities could open, stationed inspectors at every plant, and imposed fines of up to $100,000 a day or criminal charges for violations. It also protected workers who reported safety problems from retaliation. The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at DOE nuclear weapons plants — including employees of private contractors — would gain occupational safety standards, unannounced inspections, and protection from retaliation for reporting hazards. People living near plants like Savannah River, Pantex, and the Nevada Test Site would gain enforceable environmental cleanup standards, public hearings before new facilities open, and immediate notification of accidental radioactive releases. Citizens would get formal petition procedures to force board action.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Weapons plant workers and nearby residents

how_it_helps.text: Gives the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board power to write binding occupational health and safety standards covering federal and contractor employees at DOE weapons plants, ending the situation where the agency running the plants policed itself.

Requires new or substantially modified DOE defense nuclear facilities to obtain a board license before starting operations, with published notice, a public hearing, and other public participation before a license is granted.

Lets the board issue administrative orders and sue in federal court to force compliance with its standards and with other federal and state safety requirements, backed by civil fines of up to $50,000 a day (up to $100,000 a day for defying a court order) and criminal penalties including prison time.

Requires an onsite board staff for investigation and compliance at every DOE defense nuclear facility, authorizes unannounced inspections, and requires the Energy Secretary to notify the board and Congress immediately of any abnormal occurrence that could release radioactive or hazardous materials.

Requires enforcement procedures to protect individuals who file complaints from retribution, and establishes citizen petition and public hearing procedures for board action on standards, investigations, and enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: The Department of Energy and the private contractors operating its weapons plants would bear compliance costs, licensing requirements, daily fines, and the possibility of court-ordered shutdowns of unsafe operations. Taxpayers would fund a much larger board — the bill removes the existing cap of 100 full-time staff — including onsite inspection teams at every facility. Weapons plant construction and operations could face delays.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the President override board orders, board lawsuits, or court decisions at a specified facility to protect national security, with an exemption lasting up to a year that can be renewed with a new order and is largely not subject to judicial review — a significant carve-out that could hollow out enforcement when it matters most.

The bill removes the existing statutory cap of 100 full-time board employees, requires onsite staff at every facility, and adds licensing and penalty programs, so it represents a substantial expansion of federal staffing and spending on oversight.
The Energy Department formally opposed the bill, filing an unfavorable executive comment in August 1990, indicating the agency saw the compliance and licensing regime as burdensome to its mission.

The bill exempts the Waste Isolation Pilot Project from the new licensing requirement and leaves the naval nuclear propulsion program outside the definition of covered facilities entirely, limiting its reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: enforceable safety standards, inspections, and fines for weapons plants against higher compliance costs and a bigger federal oversight bureaucracy. The bill is thoughtfully designed — it defers to existing environmental laws rather than duplicating them, adds citizen and whistleblower protections, and lets the board distinguish between old and new facilities. Its main structural weakness is the presidential national security override, which could suspend enforcement at any single facility for renewable one-year periods with little judicial review. Overall, the protections for plant workers and fence-line communities outweigh the compliance costs, which fall mostly on the Energy Department and its contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees in late 1989 and never came up for a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative David Skaggs of Colorado introduced the bill on November 21, 1989, joined by 11 cosponsors including 10 Democrats and 1 Republican, Marge Roukema of New Jersey.

The bill was referred jointly to the House Armed Services and Energy and Commerce Committees, then in December 1989 to subcommittees handling military nuclear systems, transportation of hazardous materials, and energy and power.
The committee requested the Energy Department's official view; on August 1, 1990, the Department filed an unfavorable executive comment.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Energy Department and the private contractors running its nuclear weapons plants, who went on without an independent regulator empowered to fine them, inspect without notice, or shut down unsafe operations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DOE and its weapons plant contractors

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — 10 of 257 House Democrats and 1 of 175 House Republicans — and no vote was ever taken, so the chambers' actual split is unknown.

industries.note: Private companies operating DOE plants such as Savannah River, Pantex, and the Nevada Test Site would have faced licensing before startups, unannounced inspections, civil fines up to $100,000 a day, and criminal penalties — costs of avoiding enforcement fell on them. Their interest in avoiding enforcement ran against plant workers and nearby residents.

The bill would have stripped DOE's self-regulation: an outside board could set standards, license facilities, station onsite inspectors, and sue DOE in court. DOE registered its opposition through an unfavorable executive comment.

industries.industry: Independent safety regulators and environmental agencies
industries.note: The board itself would have gained staff, licensing authority, and enforcement power, and the bill explicitly preserved the authority of EPA and state agencies over DOE facilities.
